artiest/parliament.text:
Parliament was an American funk band centred on the singer and producer George Clinton. The group grew out of The Parliaments, a doo-wop group from Plainfield, New Jersey, who had a hit in 1967 with (I Wanna) Testify. From 1968 Clinton worked with two bands at once, Parliament and Funkadelic, made up largely of the same musicians. Together they were known as P-Funk. Funkadelic was the rougher, rock-oriented side, Parliament the more commercial one, with horns, synthesizers and a science-fiction world of its own.

The breakthrough came after Clinton revived the name in 1974 on the Casablanca label. On Mothership Connection (1975), black Americans land in a spaceship to bring funk down to earth. On stage, a huge spaceship, the Mothership, descended from above. The single Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof off the Sucker), written by Clinton, Bootsy Collins and Jerome Brailey, was released in April 1976. It reached number 5 on the American soul chart and number 15 on the Hot 100, and became the group's first million-seller. On Flash Light (1977), the keyboard player Bernie Worrell built the bass line from several Minimoogs.

In 1997 sixteen members of Parliament-Funkadelic were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Hip hop used their grooves as building material: on Who Am I? (What's My Name?) (1993), Snoop Doggy Dogg re-created part of Give Up the Funk. The mix of black music and space travel is an early example of Afrofuturism. In Detroit, the DJ The Electrifying Mojo played Parliament alongside Kraftwerk, and techno grew out of that combination. A replica of the Mothership now stands in the Smithsonian museum of African American history in Washington.
artiest/parliament.listen: In Give Up the Funk, listen to the voices: a deep bass voice opens, then several choirs sing over one another and answer each other ('We want the funk'). Underneath, a single tight groove on bass and drums keeps going, so that all the attention goes to the interplay of the voices.

artiest/pascal-roge.text:
Pascal Rogé, born on 6 April 1951, is a French pianist. He plays mainly the music of fellow countrymen such as Saint-Saëns, Fauré, Debussy, Ravel, Satie and Poulenc, but his repertoire also includes Haydn, Mozart, Brahms and Beethoven. His first public performance was in 1960, with Debussy's Préludes. He won the piano prize of the Paris Conservatoire and worked for years with Julius Katchen. At seventeen he gave his first recitals in major European cities and received an exclusive contract with Decca.

Rogé has a special affinity with the French composers Debussy, Fauré, Ravel and Poulenc. He also plays chamber music, with the Pasquier Trio and with musicians such as Pierre Amoyal and Michel Portal. With Portal he recorded Poulenc and Tchaikovsky. His recordings include A Liszt Recital from 1970, Claude Debussy: Piano Works Vol 1 from 1978, 3 Gymnopédies & Other Piano Works from 1984 and After the Rain… The Soft Sounds of Erik Satie from 1995. He gives recitals all over the world and is a friend of the conductor Charles Dutoit.

For anyone seeking the link between classical and popular music, Rogé is important as an interpreter of Satie and Debussy, whose clear, colourful piano music later had a great influence on jazz pianists and pop composers. For many listeners, his recordings are a first introduction to that French piano sound.
artiest/pascal-roge.listen: Listen to Satie's Gymnopédie No. 1 in his recording and notice the slow, soft chords and the simple melody above them. Hear how few notes are needed to create an almost floating atmosphere.

artiest/passport.text:
Passport was a German jazz fusion group led by the saxophonist Klaus Doldinger. The band was formed in 1971 and released its first record the same year. In the late 1960s Doldinger had presented his quartet under the pseudonym Paul Nero, playing blues rock and soul. Passport grew out of his commercial project Motherhood. On the first album, as with Motherhood, the then unknown Udo Lindenberg played drums.

The line-up changed often over the years. The group that brought the band European and international fame in the mid-1970s consisted of Doldinger, the drummer Curt Cress, the guitarist and bassist Wolfgang Schmid and the keyboard player Kristian Schultze. With albums produced by Siggi Loch and released by Atlantic Records, and with their live concerts, Doldinger made an impression with catchy melodic lines over a compelling groove. Between 1973 and 1976 the band recorded a soul-influenced, popular jazz. Albums from that period include Hand Made in 1973, Cross-Collateral in 1975 and Infinity Machine in 1976, followed by Iguaçu in 1977 and Garden of Eden in 1979. From 1977 the line-up changed. With Elmer Louis on percussion and Roy Louis on guitar, the music became more Latin jazz-oriented and more graceful. In 2006 Doldinger performed again to mark the band's thirty-fifth anniversary, with Schmid on electric bass.

Because the band was so influential, it is compared with the American group Weather Report. Passport shows that the jazz rock of the 1970s did not come only from America, and that German musicians made their own melodic version of it.
artiest/passport.listen: Listen to a track from Cross-Collateral and notice the catchy saxophone melody over the tight groove of bass and drums. Hear how jazz and funk meet.

artiest/pat-boone.text:
Pat Boone is an American singer, born in 1934 in Jacksonville, Florida, and raised in Nashville. He began performing at Sunday concerts in a park in Nashville and made records from 1953. In 1955 he signed with Dot Records.

His version of Fats Domino's Ain't That a Shame became a hit in 1955 and set the pattern for his early work: he re-recorded rhythm and blues songs by black artists for a mainly white audience. Tutti Frutti and Long Tall Sally by Little Richard followed in the same way. His versions were tidier and tamer than the originals. Critics see this as the whitewashing of black music, because it brought the original artists less recognition. Boone had 38 top 40 hits in America, six of them number ones, such as Love Letters in the Sand and April Love (1957). He sold almost fifty million records.

Boone kept up a safe, wholesome image, which worked well for advertisers. From 1957 to 1960 he hosted his own television show, sponsored by Chevrolet, and he appeared in films such as April Love and Journey to the Center of the Earth (1959). Later he turned to gospel and Christian music. In 1997 he surprised people with In a Metal Mood: No More Mr. Nice Guy, an album of heavy metal songs. In pop history, Boone stands for the way the music industry in the 1950s first sold rock 'n' roll to the general public in a tame, white version.
artiest/pat-boone.listen: First listen to Fats Domino's Ain't That a Shame, then to Pat Boone's version. Notice the difference in the singing: Domino sings loose and relaxed, Boone neatly and with careful articulation. Do you also hear how much smoother the accompaniment sounds on Boone's record?

artiest/pat-metheny.text: The guitarist Pat Metheny, from Missouri, was already teaching at Berklee in Boston at the age of nineteen. He played in the group of the vibraphonist Gary Burton and in 1976 made Bright Size Life for ECM, with Jaco Pastorius. From 1977 he led the Pat Metheny Group with the keyboard player Lyle Mays, with a spacious sound, guitar synthesizer and Brazilian influences. Ornette Coleman was one of his great role models; in 1986 he recorded Song X with him. Metheny has won twenty Grammys, across twelve different categories. He also plays acoustic and free music, and works with instruments built especially for him.
artiest/pat-metheny.listen: Hear the warm guitar above synthesizers and Brazilian rhythms.

artiest/pat-metheny-group.text:
The Pat Metheny Group was an American jazz fusion band founded in 1977 by the guitarist and composer Pat Metheny together with the pianist and keyboard player Lyle Mays. Metheny had made his name in the mid-1970s with two solo albums. For his own group he brought in Mays, who wrote most of the repertoire with him. The bassist Steve Rodby joined in 1981 and stayed until the end in 2010. The drummer Paul Wertico played with the group from 1983 to 2001.

The debut Pat Metheny Group was released in 1978. American Garage from 1979 reached number one on Billboard's jazz chart. With Offramp (1982), the Brazilian percussionist Naná Vasconcelos entered the picture, and with him the influence of South American music. That influence grew with First Circle (1984), on which the Argentine multi-instrumentalist Pedro Aznar played, and remained strongly present through Still Life (Talking) (1987) and Letter From Home (1989), with bossa nova and samba rhythms. In 1985 the group made This Is Not America with David Bowie for the film music of The Falcon and the Snowman. The single reached number one in the Netherlands.

The sound revolves around Metheny's lyrical guitar, often with a guitar synthesizer, and around Mays's piano and synthesizers. In the 1990s hip hop drum loops, free improvisation and symphonic passages were added, on albums such as Quartet and Imaginary Day. The final album, The Way Up from 2005, is a single through-composed piece lasting 68 minutes. The group showed that jazz fusion could sound melodic, world-music-minded and accessible.
artiest/pat-metheny-group.listen: Listen to Minuano (Six Eight) from Still Life (Talking). Notice how a sombre minor-key passage turns into a jubilant melody, and how the guitar solo leads into an intricate marimba section.

artiest/pat-patrick.text:
Laurdine Kenneth Patrick Jr., known as Pat Patrick, was born in 1929 in East Moline, Illinois. He played baritone saxophone, alto saxophone and electric bass and was known for his forty-year association with Sun Ra. As a child he learned piano, drums and trumpet before switching to saxophone. At DuSable High School in Chicago he met the future bassist Richard Davis and the saxophonists John Gilmore and Clifford Jordan. Even at school he was the baritone saxophonist in the house band of the Regal Theater.

Around 1950 Patrick first played in a Sun Ra band, and from 1954 he was a permanent member of the Arkestra. In 1961 the Arkestra moved to New York, where the musicians lived together in communal houses. Patrick also played with John Coltrane, including on Africa/Brass in 1961, with Blue Mitchell, with Mongo Santamaría and, in the early 1970s, with Thelonious Monk. He wrote Yeh, Yeh, which Santamaría recorded. In 1972 he co-founded the Baritone Saxophone Retinue, a group with several baritone saxophonists and a rhythm section, which recorded two albums for Saturn Records.

Patrick was a well-trained, versatile soloist and ensemble player. Besides baritone saxophone he played flute, bass and percussion. He toured Europe with Sun Ra in 1970 and 1976, taught at the State University of New York at Old Westbury and returned to the Arkestra from 1986 to 1988. He died of leukaemia in 1991. His son Deval Patrick became governor of Massachusetts.
artiest/pat-patrick.listen: In a recording by the Sun Ra Arkestra, listen for the low horns beneath the other instruments. Try to hear how the baritone saxophone gives the horn section a heavy foundation.

artiest/patricia-quinn.text:
Patricia Quinn was born in 1944 in Belfast and is a Northern Irish actress and singer. She left Northern Ireland for London at seventeen, worked as a Playboy Bunny in Mayfair and in 1969 trained at the Drama Centre London. At first she mainly played small parts in theatre, film and television. Her breakthrough came when she joined the original cast of the play The Rocky Horror Show, in 1973 at the Royal Court Theatre in London.

In the 1975 film The Rocky Horror Picture Show she played Magenta again. The role stayed with her for the rest of her career. In the film's opening scene only her lips are seen, apparently singing the opening song Science Fiction/Double Feature. The singing voice is in fact that of Richard O'Brien, the writer of the show and an actor in it. Those lips also became the emblem of the production. After its success came roles in series such as The Love School and I, Claudius, and in the 1981 film Shock Treatment, the semi-sequel to Rocky Horror. In 2012 she appeared in The Lords of Salem.

Quinn is above all an actress, not a pop star, but her role belongs to the history of the rock musical. The Rocky Horror Show grew into a cult phenomenon, and for years Quinn appeared at anniversary performances and conventions, where she sang Science Fiction/Double Feature herself.
artiest/patricia-quinn.listen: Listen to Science Fiction/Double Feature from The Rocky Horror Picture Show. Notice how the song begins as a playful, old-fashioned-sounding opening number, while on screen Quinn's lips seem to sing in a different voice.

artiest/patrick-cowley.text:
Patrick Cowley was born in 1950 in Buffalo, New York State. As a teenager he was a drummer in amateur bands and studied English. In 1971 he moved to San Francisco, where he studied music at City College, with an emphasis on synthesizers. In 1978 he met the singer Sylvester, who asked him to strengthen his studio band after hearing early synthesizer recordings by him. Cowley played synthesizer on the album Step II, with the hits You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real) and Dance (Disco Heat), and wrote songs for the album Stars. He also toured with Sylvester's live band.

In 1981 he had success of his own with Menergy and Megatron Man, which ranked high in the American dance charts. Menergy is a frank tribute to the city's gay club scene, and the parties at The EndUp carried that name. He also wrote and produced Right on Target for Paul Parker, and made Do Ya Wanna Funk with Sylvester. In 1978 he built a remix of Donna Summer's I Feel Love of more than fifteen minutes, working from an ordinary record because he did not have the original master tapes. That remix has become a sought-after collector's item.

Alongside Giorgio Moroder, Cowley is regarded as a pioneer of electronic dance music. His style, Hi-NRG, is fast, synthetic and built for the dance floor. He made his last album, Mind Warp, when he already felt the effects of HIV. He died in November 1982, aged thirty-two.
artiest/patrick-cowley.listen: Listen to Menergy. Notice the fast, driving synthesizer lines and how the beat runs on relentlessly, made for a night in the club.

artiest/patrick-doyle.text: Patrick Doyle was born in 1953 in Uddingston, Scotland. He graduated from the Royal Scottish Academy of Music in 1975. In 1987 he became composer and musical director of Kenneth Branagh's Renaissance Theatre Company. A long collaboration grew out of this. For Branagh he wrote, among others, Henry V (1989), Much Ado About Nothing (1993), Hamlet (1996), Thor (2011) and Cinderella (2015). Sense and Sensibility (1995) and Hamlet earned him Oscar nominations. In Sense and Sensibility the soprano Jane Eaglen sings two songs. He also wrote Gosford Park (2001), Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005) and Pixar's Brave (2012). In 1997 he contracted leukaemia. He kept writing in hospital and made a full recovery.
artiest/patrick-doyle.listen: Notice the long, singing melodies in the strings and woodwinds, and how in Brave Doyle weaves Scottish folk colours such as bagpipes and fiddle into the orchestra.

artiest/patsy-cline.text:
Patsy Cline was born Virginia Patterson Hensley in 1932 in Winchester, Virginia. At fifteen she was already singing on the local radio station WINC. In 1954 she signed with the label 4 Star, and in 1957 she won the talent contest Arthur Godfrey's Talent Scouts on American television with Walkin' After Midnight. The song became her first big hit, on both the country chart and the pop chart. After that, success failed to follow. In 1958 she moved to Nashville, became a member of the Grand Ole Opry and in 1960 switched to Decca Records.

Under the guidance of the producer Owen Bradley her sound changed and success returned. I Fall to Pieces from 1961 was her first single to reach the top of the country chart. After a serious car accident came Crazy, which also became a big hit. Later came, among others, She's Got You and Leavin' on Your Mind. Her albums from those years are Patsy Cline (1957), Showcase (1961) and Sentimentally Yours (1962).

Cline was one of the first country singers to succeed in reaching an audience in the pop world. On 5 March 1963 she died in a plane crash, aged thirty. In 1973 she became the first woman inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame. She is regarded as a forerunner for women in country music, who could take the lead role on records and in concerts.
artiest/patsy-cline.listen: Listen to Crazy and notice how Cline lets the melody flow unhurried. Try to hear how her voice carries the song, without the accompaniment pushing itself forward.

artiest/patti-smith.text:
Patti Smith was born in 1946 in Chicago and grew into a singer, songwriter, poet and writer. In New York she became one of the faces of the punk scene. Her debut album Horses from 1975 made her influential and earned her the nicknames Queen of Punk and Godmother of Punk. Smith brought rock and poetry together: she worked as a poet and writer, and you can hear that in her lyrics.

Her best-known song is Because the Night from 1978, which she co-wrote with Bruce Springsteen. It reached number thirteen on the American Hot 100 and number five in Britain. Later came albums such as Dream of Life (1988), Gone Again (1996), Peace and Noise (1997), Gung Ho (2000), Trampin' (2003) and Banga (2012). In 2010 she won the National Book Award for Just Kids, her memoir about her friend and former partner, the photographer Robert Mapplethorpe. She wrote the book to keep a promise to him.

Smith was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2007 and received the Polar Music Prize in 2011. She showed that a rock record can also be literature, and brought that to the fore in the New York punk scene.
artiest/patti-smith.listen: Listen to Because the Night and pay attention to the vocals. Try to hear how Smith sings the chorus with total commitment.

artiest/patty-andrews.text:
Patty Andrews was the youngest of the three sisters who together formed the Andrews Sisters, an American close-harmony group from the swing era. She was born in 1918 in Minneapolis and sang the lead part. Her sisters were LaVerne, contralto, and Maxene, soprano. The sisters began as imitators of the Boswell Sisters, travelled the country with bands and in vaudeville, and in 1937 gained national attention with Bei Mir Bist Du Schön, a Yiddish song that was translated into English and released on Decca.

One hit followed another, with Beer Barrel Polka (Roll Out the Barrel) in 1939, Beat Me Daddy, Eight to the Bar in 1940 and Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy in 1941, an early example of jump blues. During the Second World War they performed for soldiers, sang in films such as Buck Privates and made records with Bing Crosby. In 1945 came Rum and Coca-Cola, based on a calypso from Trinidad, which introduced American listeners to the genre. The arranger Vic Schoen played a large part in their sound.

In the 1950s Patty began a solo career and temporarily split from her sisters. The group reunited in 1956, but the success of old did not return. Her sisters died in 1967 and 1995, Patty in 2013. Their voices have been emulated by Bette Midler, The Pointer Sisters and Christina Aguilera.
artiest/patty-andrews.listen: Listen to Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy. Notice how the three voices sing so close together that they form a single sound, and how the boogie-woogie bass drives the rhythm.

artiest/paul-agnew.text:
Paul Agnew was born in 1964 in Glasgow and is a Scottish tenor and conductor. He studied music as a choral scholar at Magdalen College, Oxford. There he entered the world of early music and sang with ensembles such as Ex Cathedra, the Consort of Musicke, The Tallis Scholars, The Sixteen and Gothic Voices, before beginning a solo career in the early 1990s. He is known for his high tenor roles in the French repertoire, although he also sings other works.

His recordings include Mozart's Coronation Mass, cantatas and the B minor Mass by Bach with Ton Koopman, the St John Passion with Stephen Cleobury, Berlioz's L'enfance du Christ with Philippe Herreweghe and Handel's Solomon with Paul McCreesh. He sang the title role in Rameau's Platée, which was released on DVD. As a soloist he worked above all with William Christie and Les Arts Florissants, singing in productions of Charpentier and Rameau. Rameau's Grands Motets won the Gramophone award for best early vocal music recording in 1995.

In 2013 Agnew became associate musical director of Les Arts Florissants and co-founded the academy Le Jardin des Voix. In 2007 he conducted the ensemble for the first time in a Vivaldi performance, as the first conductor alongside William Christie. Since 2020 he has been co-musical director. He combines singing and conducting, and recorded a series of albums of Italian madrigals.
artiest/paul-agnew.listen: Listen to a recording of Agnew in the French Baroque repertoire. Notice how clear and high his tenor sounds and how smoothly he follows the long lines.

artiest/paul-bley.text:
Paul Bley was born in 1932 in Montreal and became a Canadian jazz pianist who made his name through his work in free jazz. As a child he played the violin, but he switched to piano. He studied at the Juilliard School in New York. In 1953 he brought Charlie Parker to the Montreal Jazz Workshop, where they recorded together. The album Introducing Paul Bley from 1954 was his debut. In the 1950s he played in trios and with, among others, Lester Young, Chet Baker and Ben Webster, and in Los Angeles his quintet featured Ornette Coleman, Don Cherry, Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins.

In the 1960s Bley played in a trio with Jimmy Giuffre and Steve Swallow that combined chamber music and free jazz. In 1964 he was involved in the founding of the Jazz Composers Guild in New York. In 1969 he gave the first live concert on Moog and ARP synthesizers in New York. In 1972 Open, to Love appeared, his first solo record for ECM. On Improvising Artists, the label he founded in 1974, he released the album Jaco, the debut of Pat Metheny on electric guitar alongside Jaco Pastorius on bass.

In 1955 Bley said that he wanted to write music without a chord centre. He was influential for trio playing and for jazz with electronics. He died in Florida in 2016.
artiest/paul-bley.listen: Listen to Open, to Love. Notice how Bley creates space with the piano alone, with silence between the notes and no fixed rhythm.

artiest/paul-butterfield.text:
Paul Butterfield was born in 1942 in Chicago and grew up in the Hyde Park neighbourhood. He first learned classical flute, but a knee injury and his growing love of the blues set him on a different path. He became a harmonica player and singer and found his way into the blues clubs of Chicago, where Muddy Waters encouraged him and let him sit in. With the guitarist Elvin Bishop he formed a band in 1963 with the bassist Jerome Arnold and the drummer Sam Lay, both from Howlin' Wolf's band. After a successful run of performances at the club Big John's, the guitarist Mike Bloomfield joined and the group signed with Elektra Records.

The Paul Butterfield Blues Band released its debut album The Paul Butterfield Blues Band in 1965. In 1966 came East-West, on which the band also showed jazz influences. The Resurrection of Pigboy Crabshaw (1967) reached the highest position of any of his albums in the American chart. The band played at the Monterey Pop Festival and at Woodstock. Later he also recorded with his mentor Muddy Waters and with members of The Band. Butterfield died in 1987.

The group combined electric Chicago blues with the ferocity of rock and was one of the first racially mixed blues bands. This brought the blues to a young, white and wider audience. Butterfield is regarded as one of the best-known blues harp players. In 2006 he was inducted into the Blues Hall of Fame, and in 2015 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame followed for him and the first band members.
artiest/paul-butterfield.listen: Listen to Born in Chicago by The Paul Butterfield Blues Band. Notice how the harmonica takes the lead as a solo instrument, in an electric blues band full of energy.

artiest/paul-chambers.text: The bassist Paul Chambers grew up in Detroit, where there was a rich jazz scene. In 1955, aged twenty, he joined the first quintet of Miles Davis, with whom he stayed until 1963; he therefore also played on Kind of Blue. He also played on dozens of other records for Blue Note and Prestige. His walking bass was firm and precise, and he also often soloed with the bow. John Coltrane wrote the piece Mr. P.C. for him, which appears on Giant Steps. Chambers drank heavily and used drugs; he died of tuberculosis in 1969, aged 33.
artiest/paul-chambers.listen: Follow the bass: an even stream of notes on every beat.

artiest/paul-de-munnik.text:
Paul de Munnik is a Dutch singer, actor and cabaret performer, born in 1970 in Dronten. As a boy he sang in his mother's church choir and played in a new age band. At the Kleinkunstacademie (the Dutch academy for cabaret and small-scale theatre) in Amsterdam he met Thomas Acda in 1989. Their graduation show Spectacle Coupé won the Pisuisse Prize in 1993.

In 1995 they came together again for the show Zwerf'On, and the duo Acda en de Munnik grew out of it. Their theatre programmes always turned into albums: the debut Acda en De Munnik (1997), Naar huis (1998), which reached number 1 in the album chart, and later, among others, Groeten uit Maaiveld (2003) and Nachtmuziek (2007). The breakthrough came in 1998 with the summer hit Niet of nooit geweest, which reached number two in the Top 40. Het regent zonnestralen did not make the chart, but later became one of their most popular songs. De Munnik sings and plays piano. Characteristic of the duo is the harmony singing of the two voices, in often melancholy songs about love, friendship, life and death. In 1997 they received the Zilveren Harp.

In 2015 they said farewell with a tour that ended at Carré, but in 2023 they returned, with concerts at Ahoy, the Ziggo Dome and the Olympic Stadium. Besides this, De Munnik pursued his own projects, such as the show Op weg naar huis (2007), a programme built around the songs of Jacques Brel, and a solo album. He also acted in television series such as Pleidooi and Help.
artiest/paul-de-munnik.listen: In Niet of nooit geweest, listen to how the two voices take turns in the verses and sing together in the chorus. Notice how simple the accompaniment stays, so that the singing and the lyrics come first.

artiest/paul-desmond.text:
Paul Desmond, born Paul Emil Breitenfeld, was an American alto saxophonist and composer, born in 1924 in San Francisco. He was one of the most important figures of Cool Jazz and one of the best-known saxophonists of West Coast jazz.

From 1951 until the end of 1967 Desmond played in the Dave Brubeck Quartet. For that group he wrote Take Five, which appeared in 1959 on the album Time Out. The piece is in 5/4 time, unusual for jazz at the time, and became the best-selling jazz track ever. Desmond stipulated in his will that the proceeds should go to the Red Cross. In the quartet, his light, airy saxophone formed a contrast with the heavier piano playing of Brubeck, who often used several keys at once.

Desmond himself said that he wanted to sound like a dry martini: clear, light and without unnecessary ornament. His improvisations are praised for their logical construction and their singing quality, and he was known for his high notes. Outside Brubeck he made two albums with the baritone saxophonist Gerry Mulligan, Blues in Time (1957) and Two of a Mind (1962), and worked a great deal with the guitarist Jim Hall. He also played with Chet Baker. Albums under his own name include Desmond Blue, Take Ten and Pure Desmond. Desmond smoked heavily and died in 1977 in New York of lung cancer, shortly after his last concert with Brubeck.
artiest/paul-desmond.listen: In Take Five, listen to Brubeck's piano figure, which keeps marking the five beats of the bar: try to count along to five. Then notice Desmond's alto sax: light, clear and without excessive vibrato, exactly the dry sound he was after.

artiest/paul-di-anno.text:
Paul Di'Anno, whose real name was Paul Andrews, was born in 1958 in Chingford, Essex, and became an English heavy metal singer. His father was Brazilian. As a teenager he sang in various rock and metal bands and worked as a butcher and a cook. He came to Iron Maiden through the drummer Doug Sampson, an old friend of the bassist and founder Steve Harris. From 1978 to 1981 he was the band's lead singer.

With him Iron Maiden recorded two albums: the self-titled debut Iron Maiden from 1980 and Killers from 1981, plus the live EP Maiden Japan. The debut is regarded as a classic of the genre. On it the band combined the energy of punk with the riffs of metal and the complexity of progressive rock. That became a model for later thrash metal and speed metal. Di'Anno's drug use made him increasingly unreliable in 1981, and Iron Maiden looked for a singer who could cope with a long tour. His place went to Bruce Dickinson, formerly of Samson. His last performance with the band was on 10 September 1981 in Copenhagen.

Afterwards Di'Anno made countless records, as a solo artist and with bands such as Di'Anno, Gogmagog, Battlezone, Killers and Praying Mantis. His first project after Maiden sounded more American, in the direction of Journey and Foreigner. He died in 2024. His singing from those years is part of the sound with which Iron Maiden began.
artiest/paul-di-anno.listen: Listen to Remember Tomorrow by Iron Maiden. Notice Di'Anno's singing, and how punk energy and metal riffs come together.

artiest/paul-dukas.text:
Paul Dukas was born in 1865 in Paris and was a French composer, critic and teacher. He studied at the Conservatoire de Paris, where he came second in the Prix de Rome, but not first. Disappointed, he left the conservatoire in 1889. After that he combined composing with work as a music critic for French periodicals. Dukas was a perfectionist with a reserved character. Out of dissatisfaction he destroyed much of his own work, so that only a few pieces have survived.

His best-known composition is L'apprenti sorcier from 1897, a scherzo for orchestra of ten to twelve minutes based on Goethe's poem Der Zauberlehrling. The piece became his best-known work and achieved worldwide fame, above all through Disney's 1940 film Fantasia. Dukas himself was irritated by its popularity. He also wrote the Symphony in C (1895 to 1896), the opera Ariane et Barbe-bleue, a piano sonata, the Variations, Interlude et Finale sur un thème de Rameau and the ballet La Péri.

At a time when French musicians were divided into conservatives and innovators, Dukas belonged to neither camp and kept the admiration of both. His music shows the influence of, among others, Beethoven, Berlioz, Franck, d'Indy and Debussy. Later he taught composition. His pupils included Olivier Messiaen, Maurice Duruflé, Joaquín Rodrigo and Walter Piston.
artiest/paul-dukas.listen: Listen to L'apprenti sorcier. Notice how the orchestra tells a story without words and how the same melody keeps returning in a different tone colour.

artiest/paul-elstak.text:
Paul Elstak was born in 1966 in The Hague and grew up in a musical family. His father played rhythm guitar in a band, and the well-known jazz musician Nedly Elstak was also part of the family. The money he earned as a teenager picking tomatoes and working at McDonald's he spent on records, which he practised with for hours behind the turntables. In 1987 he became a DJ at the Rotterdam discotheque Bluetiek-In. There he learned a great deal from the house pioneer Peter Slaghuis.

In 1991, as Holy Noise with Rob Fabrie, he had a top hit with James Brown is still alive. He specialised in hardcore house with very hard beats. In 1992 he started Rotterdam Records, the first hardcore label in the Netherlands. With it he reached number two in the Top 40 with Poing! by Rotterdam Termination Source. At the end of 1994 happy hardcore emerged, with fast, cheerful melody lines and vocals. That variant suited the radio and brought him a string of hits. In 1995 he had a top ten hit with Life Is Like A Dance, made with the Klubbheads. That year he also received the Zilveren Harp. The album May the Forze Be With You was released in 1995.

Elstak is one of the best-known Dutch DJs of the hardcore scene. With his label Offensive Records, from 2001, he was able to focus fully on gabber music again. In 2024 he co-wrote and co-produced Europapa by Joost Klein, the Dutch entry for the Eurovision Song Contest. The course cites his track Luv U More from 1994 as an example of the happy hardcore with which he reached a large audience.
artiest/paul-elstak.listen: Listen to Luv U More. Notice the high tempo, the hard bass and the cheerful melody singing over the beats.

artiest/paul-epworth.text:
Paul Epworth was born in 1974 in Bishop's Stortford and is an English producer and musician. He began as the singer and guitarist of the band Lomax from 2002 to 2004 and made remixes under the name Phones, with which he attracted attention through his remix of Bloc Party's Banquet. His first real production work came in 2004 and 2005, with, among others, Bloc Party's Silent Alarm and Maxïmo Park's A Certain Trigger, two albums that were nominated for the Mercury Music Prize, and the debut by The Futureheads.

His breakthrough as a writer and producer came in 2007 with Kate Nash's Made of Bricks, on which he co-wrote Foundations. In 2009 he co-produced Lungs, the debut album by Florence and the Machine, featuring Rabbit Heart (Raise It Up). Later he worked with Adele and Rihanna, and for Skyfall he won an Oscar for best original song. He won three Brit Awards as best British producer, the last in 2015, and seven Grammys. In 2020 he released his own debut album Voyager.

Epworth founded the independent label Wolf Tone, which released music by Glass Animals and The Horrors. He is a good example of the producer who became ever more important in pop history: he co-writes, shapes the sound and gives records their character.
artiest/paul-epworth.listen: Listen to Rabbit Heart (Raise It Up) by Florence and the Machine. Notice how vocals and production together build the song.

artiest/paul-gonsalves.text:
Paul Gonsalves was born in 1920 in Brockton, Massachusetts, the son of Portuguese-Cape Verdean parents. He began on guitar and as a child played Cape Verdean folk songs for his family. He grew up in New Bedford and played tenor saxophone in the orchestra of Sabby Lewis. In the 1940s he also played with Cape Verdean American colleagues in the band of Phil Edmund. Then came the big bands of Count Basie, from 1947 to 1949, and of Dizzy Gillespie. In 1950 he joined the orchestra of Duke Ellington, where he became a regular soloist.

His greatest moment came at the Newport Jazz Festival in 1956. In Ellington's Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue, Gonsalves played a solo of 27 choruses. The attention that performance drew is said to have revived Ellington's faltering career of the 1950s. The recording is on the album Ellington at Newport. Gonsalves was the soloist in numerous Ellington pieces and was given the nickname The Strolling Violins by Ellington, because he walked through the audience during his solos.

He also recorded under his own name, including Tenor Stuff (1961) and Salt and Pepper (1963). Gonsalves died in 1974 in London, ten days before Ellington himself. Mercer Ellington did not dare tell his father the news, for fear that the shock would speed up his decline.
artiest/paul-gonsalves.listen: Listen to Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue on Ellington at Newport. Notice how the tenor saxophone builds ever higher in the solo and how the audience reacts to it more and more.

artiest/paul-hillier.text:
Paul Hillier was born in 1949 in Dorchester and is an English conductor, singer and baritone. In 1967 he began studying voice at the Guildhall School of Music & Drama in London. In 1974 he founded the Hilliard Ensemble with the tenor Paul Elliott and the countertenor David James, and led it until 1990. That year he started Theatre of Voices, a group that performs contemporary repertoire as well as early music. With the American ensemble His Majestie's Clerkes he recorded early American choral music, including by William Billings, on the album A Land of Pure Delight.

Hillier specialises in both early and contemporary music, above all that of Steve Reich and Arvo Pärt. He directed the Estonian Philharmonic Chamber Choir, was director of the Early Music Institute at Indiana University and from 2003 to 2023 led Ars Nova in Copenhagen. From 2008 he was artistic director of Chamber Choir Ireland. He also recorded solo albums, partly with the harpist Andrew Lawrence-King.

He also wrote and edited books, including the first English-language study of Arvo Pärt and a collection of Steve Reich's writings. In 2006 he was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire.
artiest/paul-hillier.listen: Listen to a recording by the Hilliard Ensemble, for example from the early music repertoire. Notice how a few voices without instruments form a single sound.

artiest/paul-j-smith.text:
Paul J. Smith was born in 1906 in Calumet, Michigan, and was an American composer and violinist best known for his work at Disney. He studied music at The College of Idaho and then at the Bush Conservatory of Music in Chicago. His aptitude for theory and composition won him a scholarship to Juilliard, although it is unclear whether he used it. In 1934 he joined Disney, where he remained for a large part of his life as a composer for films, animation and live action, cinema and television.

Smith received an Oscar nomination for Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. He won his only Oscar together with Leigh Harline and Ned Washington for the music of Pinocchio. Six nominations followed, for Saludos Amigos, Victory Through Air Power, The Three Caballeros, Song of the South, Cinderella and Perri. He wrote the music for most of the episodes of the True-Life Adventures, Disney's nature film series, and for more than seventy animated shorts. In Fantasia he can be seen himself as a member of the orchestra.

His music belongs to the first decades of the Disney film, when studio composers wrote scores for cartoons and nature documentaries.
artiest/paul-j-smith.listen: Listen to an excerpt from Pinocchio and notice how the music follows the movement on screen. Try to hear how an orchestra accompanies a cartoon story.

artiest/paul-jackson.text:
Paul Jackson was born in 1947 in Oakland, California, and became an American jazz bassist and composer. As a child he played piano and bassoon, and he began on the bass at the age of nine. At fourteen he was already playing with the Oakland Symphony Orchestra, and afterwards he studied at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. He became known as a founding member of the Headhunters, the group Herbie Hancock formed in 1973, with Bennie Maupin on saxophone and clarinet, Harvey Mason on drums and Bill Summers on percussion.

Their first album, Head Hunters from 1973, became the best-selling jazz album to that date and the first to sell a million copies. It reached number thirteen on the American Billboard 200. Jackson co-wrote the opening track Chameleon, which became a jazz standard. After that he played on Hancock's albums Thrust (1974), Man-Child (1975), Flood (1975) and Secrets (1976).

Later Jackson moved to Japan, where he started the voluntary concert series Jazz for Kids, intended to familiarise pupils with African American history. He died in 2021. His electric bass is part of the sound of Hancock's Headhunters.
artiest/paul-jackson.listen: Listen to Chameleon by Herbie Hancock and notice the bass groove. Try to hear how a repeating pattern is the foundation for the solos above it.

artiest/paul-kalkbrenner.text:
Paul Kalkbrenner is a German electronic music producer, born in 1977. He grew up in Lichtenberg, in the former East Berlin. When the Wall came down he was thirteen. Soon afterwards he was playing records in Berlin youth clubs, despite his mother's evening curfew. With his school friend Sascha Funke he immersed himself in techno between 1992 and 1997. They admired Underground Resistance from Detroit and visited clubs such as E-Werk, Planet and Walfisch. At school Kalkbrenner also learned to play the trumpet and music theory.

In 1999 his first work appeared on Ellen Allien's label BPitch Control, under the name Paul dB+. His albums Superimpose and Zeit came out in 2001. With Self in 2004, his music, which is melodic and full of big emotions, took on a narrative line. Gebrünn Gebrünn became a crossover hit. In 2008 he left BPitch Control on good terms. The director Hannes Stöhr asked him to make the music for Berlin Calling, a film about a Berlin DJ, and Kalkbrenner also played the lead role, Ickarus. The track Sky and Sand from the soundtrack became his best-known single and reached high positions in, among other places, Belgium and Germany.

Because he builds his tracks in separate parts and reassembles them on stage, Kalkbrenner is regarded as a live act rather than a DJ. Later came, among others, Icke wieder (2011), Guten Tag (2012) and Parts of Life (2018). He shows that techno from the Berlin clubs could also carry a large audience and a film.
artiest/paul-kalkbrenner.listen: Listen to Sky and Sand. Notice how the beat and the synthesizer line build up slowly and how a singing voice only joins later in the track.

artiest/paul-lovens.text:
Paul Lovens was born in 1949 in Aachen and is a German drummer and percussionist. He plays drums, percussion and cymbals, and also the singing saw, a rare instrument in music. He belongs to European free jazz and free improvisation. In the early 1970s he played in a trio with the pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach, a collaboration he continued afterwards. He also performed with the Aardvark Jazz Orchestra and the Berlin Contemporary Jazz Orchestra.

Lovens worked with many names from free music, including Cecil Taylor, Peter Brötzmann, Eugene Chadbourne, Mats Gustafsson, Thomas Lehn, Phil Wachsmann and Joëlle Léandre. He also played with Florian Schneider and Eberhard Kranemann in an early incarnation of Kraftwerk. With the drummer Paul Lytton he runs the record label Po Torch, on which many of his own albums appeared, such as Paul Rutherford / Paul Lovens (1978) and Stranger Than Love (1985).

His records appeared on, among others, FMP, Po Torch, Intakt and Acta. In the 1970s he recorded, among other things, Carpathes, with Michel Pilz and Peter Kowald. In this way Lovens has built up a long career in free improvisation.
artiest/paul-lovens.listen: Listen to a recording with Lovens. Notice how the percussion does not keep a fixed tempo, but responds to what the other musicians do.

artiest/paul-mccartney.text:
Paul McCartney was born on 18 June 1942 in Liverpool. His father played jazz, and as a teenager Paul taught himself to play piano and guitar and to write songs. Little Richard and Buddy Holly were his role models. In 1957 he joined The Quarrymen, John Lennon's skiffle group, which became The Beatles in 1960. There he played bass and keyboards and shared the songwriting and lead vocals with Lennon.

Their partnership became the most successful in music history. McCartney songs such as Yesterday, Eleanor Rigby and Blackbird are among the most covered songs ever. He immersed himself in the London avant-garde and helped bring experimental studio techniques into the music of The Beatles. From Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) he increasingly became the group's de facto leader. After the break-up he made his solo debut in 1970 with McCartney and, with his wife Linda and Denny Laine, formed the band Wings. Wings became one of the most successful bands of the 1970s, with hits such as My Love, Band on the Run and Mull of Kintyre.

McCartney is known for his melodic bass parts, his wide vocal range and his versatility. He wrote in styles ranging from pre-war pop to ballads, classical music and electronics. Later he sang duets with Stevie Wonder (Ebony and Ivory) and Michael Jackson (Say Say Say). He wrote or co-wrote 32 number ones on the American Billboard Hot 100, more than anyone else. In 1997 he was knighted.
artiest/paul-mccartney.listen: Listen to Yesterday (1965) by The Beatles. Notice how bare the song is: McCartney sings with only an acoustic guitar, and a string quartet fills in the rest, with no drums and no other Beatles.

artiest/paul-mccreesh.text:
Paul McCreesh was born in 1960 and is an English conductor. He began as a cellist and in 1981 took his bachelor's degree in music at the University of Manchester. In 1982 he founded the Gabrieli Consort and Players, of which he is artistic director. With them he has performed in concert halls and at festivals all over the world. He was also artistic director of the Wratislavia Cantans Festival in Wrocław and founded the Brinkburn Festival in England. In 2005 he received an honorary doctorate from Loughborough University.

McCreesh made his name with music from the Renaissance and the Baroque, above all from Venice. His breakthrough was the 1990 album A Venetian Coronation 1595, a reconstruction of the coronation of the doge Marino Grimani, which won a Gramophone Award. He is known for such liturgical reconstructions, in which music is presented in the context of a church service, with the ringing of bells as background sound. From 1993 he recorded extensively for Deutsche Grammophon, and in 2011 he founded the label Winged Lion.

Later he also worked with symphony orchestras and conducted operas by Handel, Gluck and Mozart. In 2020 BBC Music Magazine chose his recording of Purcell's King Arthur as recording of the year.
artiest/paul-mccreesh.listen: Listen to A Venetian Coronation 1595. Notice how the choirs and the brass evoke the space of a large church, and how the music belongs to a ceremony.

artiest/paul-motian.text:
Paul Motian was born in 1931 in Philadelphia, grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, and was an American jazz drummer, percussionist and composer of Armenian descent. As a child he played guitar; at twelve he started on drums. During the Korean War he served in the navy, where he attended the navy's music school, and afterwards he studied at the Manhattan School of Music. In 1954 he became a professional musician and briefly played with Thelonious Monk. He became known as the drummer in the trio of the pianist Bill Evans, from 1959 to 1964, first with the bassist Scott LaFaro and later with Chuck Israels.

Afterwards he played with Paul Bley and, from 1967 to 1976, with Keith Jarrett. In 1968 and 1969 he briefly played with Arlo Guthrie, including at Woodstock. From the early 1970s he became a bandleader and composer. His debut as a leader was Conception Vessel (1973) for ECM. From the early 1980s he led a trio with the guitarist Bill Frisell and the saxophonist Joe Lovano. That trio also recorded albums of the work of Monk and Evans and the series Paul Motian on Broadway. His Electric Bebop Band, formed in the early 1990s, played bebop standards with young musicians and several electric guitars.

Motian played an important part in freeing drummers from their task of keeping strict time. In his own groups there was usually no pianist but plenty of guitar. He died in 2011.
artiest/paul-motian.listen: Listen to Motian in the Bill Evans trio. Notice how the drums do not merely keep the beat, but also join in with what the piano and bass are doing.

artiest/paul-murphy.text:
Paul Murphy was born in 1949 and is an American percussionist, bandleader and composer. He began on drums at a very young age and at six met Gene Krupa, with whom he later also took lessons, as he did with Louis Bellson and with Joseph Levitt, the principal percussionist of the National Symphony Orchestra. At sixteen he played in the Washington area with Billy Taylor, the bassist of Duke Ellington, who introduced him to the music of the pianist Cecil Taylor. On his advice he moved to San Francisco, where he built up a band of his own and met Cecil Taylor and the saxophonist Jimmy Lyons.

On Lyons's suggestion he went to New York. There he managed Ali's Alley, a club run by the drummer Rashied Ali, and played and recorded with Lyons's groups and with his own quintet. In New York he moved in both experimental jazz and punk rock. After Lyons's early death in 1986 he played for a while in Las Vegas, and in San Francisco he formed Trio Hurricane with the saxophonist Glenn Spearman and the bassist William Parker. Since 1990 he has lived around Washington again, where he has worked with, among others, the pianists Joel Futterman and Larry Willis.

Reviewers called him a fluid, compositionally minded master drummer who uses all parts of the drum kit with hands, brushes, mallets and sticks. Murphy is known above all for his small jazz groups and his long collaboration with Lyons.
artiest/paul-murphy.listen: Listen to a recording of Murphy with one of his small groups, for example from the album Excursions. Notice how fluidly he moves from drum to cymbal and how lightly and quickly he can play.

artiest/paul-oakenfold.text:
Paul Oakenfold was born in 1963 in London and became an English DJ, producer and remixer. He grew up as a bedroom DJ with the Beatles as his first love, because his father played in a skiffle band. He first trained for four years as a cook. In the late 1970s he met the DJ Trevor Fung, who became his mentor. In 1981 he moved with a friend to New York, where he witnessed the rise of hip hop in clubs such as Studio 54. Back in London he worked for Champion Records and signed DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince and Salt-n-Pepa. He was also the British agent of the Beastie Boys and Run-D.M.C.

In 1987 Oakenfold travelled to Ibiza with friends. Back in England he organised an Ibiza Reunion in an English club, which grew into Spectrum, a regular acid house night at Heaven. In 1990 he worked with Steve Osborne on remixes for the Happy Mondays, including Step On, and produced their album Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches. He also played at Spike Island for the Stone Roses. Later came albums such as Bunkka (2002) and A Lively Mind (2006).

He made more than a hundred remixes for artists such as U2, Moby, Madonna, Massive Attack and Michael Jackson. In 1998 and 1999 DJ Magazine voted him the number one DJ in the world. In this way he belongs to the DJ culture that reached the public in the 1990s.
artiest/paul-oakenfold.listen: Listen to Step On by the Happy Mondays, on which Oakenfold collaborated. Notice how a guitar band sounds here with a danceable rhythm.

artiest/paul-pena.text:
Paul Pena was born in 1950 in Hyannis, Massachusetts, into a family of Cape Verdean descent. Because of congenital glaucoma he was almost blind from birth and from the age of five attended the Perkins School for the Blind. He became a singer, songwriter and guitarist, and the music of the first half of his career touched on Delta blues, jazz, morna, flamenco, folk and rock 'n' roll. In 1969 his band played in Philadelphia as the opening act for Frank Zappa and the Grateful Dead, and the same year he performed at the Newport Folk Festival.

After moving to San Francisco in 1971 he often played for Jerry Garcia and Merl Saunders. His debut album Paul Pena was released in 1972 and received good reviews but sold little. His second album, New Train, was recorded in 1973 but only released in 2000, because of a dispute with Albert Grossman of Bearsville Records. Steve Miller heard the album and recorded the song Jet Airliner for Book of Dreams in 1977. It became a big hit and the income supported Pena for years.

In 1984 Pena heard Tuvan throat singing on shortwave radio and taught himself the techniques, by his own account with memories of bluesmen such as Howlin' Wolf. His deep voice earned him the nickname Cher Shimjer, earthquake, among the Tuvans. The 1999 documentary Genghis Blues follows him in that world.
artiest/paul-pena.listen: Listen to Jet Airliner by the Steve Miller Band. Pena wrote the song himself. Notice how it sounds as a rock song, and ask yourself how much of the blues with which Pena began you can hear.

artiest/paul-simon.text:
Paul Simon was born in 1941 in Newark, New Jersey, and grew up in Queens, New York. He is an American singer-songwriter and guitarist. At primary school in 1953 he met Art Garfunkel. In the 1960s the two became known together as Simon & Garfunkel, with a blend of folk and rock and hits such as The Sound of Silence (1965), Mrs. Robinson (1968), America (1968) and The Boxer (1969). Their last album, Bridge over Troubled Water from 1970, is among the best-selling albums ever.

As a solo artist Simon tried, among other things, gospel, reggae and soul. The albums Paul Simon (1972), There Goes Rhymin' Simon (1973) and Still Crazy After All These Years (1975) produced hits such as Mother and Child Reunion, Me and Julio Down by the Schoolyard, Kodachrome and 50 Ways to Leave Your Lover. In 1981 he played the Concert in Central Park with Garfunkel. In 1986 came Graceland, his most successful album, with South African influences. You Can Call Me Al became one of his biggest singles. Then came The Rhythm of the Saints (1990) and a second concert in the park in 1991 without Garfunkel, which drew about 500,000 people. The musical The Capeman from 1998 was poorly received.

Simon was inducted twice into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and won sixteen Grammys, including three for Album of the Year. Graceland is in the National Recording Registry. He made his acting debut in Woody Allen's Annie Hall and co-founded the Children's Health Fund.
artiest/paul-simon.listen: Listen to You Can Call Me Al from Graceland. Notice the South African influence in the guitars and the rhythm.

artiest/paul-simon-en-ladysmith-black-ma.text:
This is a meeting between an American singer and a South African choir. In 1986 Paul Simon recorded the album Graceland, and Ladysmith Black Mambazo sang on it. For the group it meant their international breakthrough. Their male voices can be heard in Homeless, the song the course cites.

Ladysmith Black Mambazo is a male choir that sings the South African styles isicathamiya and mbube. Joseph Shabalala founded the first group in December 1960, with relatives he knew from the farm where he grew up. In 1964, for half a year, he had the same dream again and again of a choir singing in perfect harmony. He re-formed the group with younger relatives and taught them those harmonies. The result included the song Nomathemba. The group took part in Saturday-night competitions in the hostels of Durban and Johannesburg and won almost everything. After that Shabalala changed the name. Ladysmith is his family's home town, the black ox is regarded as the strongest farm animal, and mambazo is the Zulu word for axe, an image for cutting down the competition. In the early 1970s the choir was no longer allowed to enter the competitions, because it kept winning. It did continue to perform, and from 1967 it was heard on the radio. In 1972 it signed with the Gallo Record Company.

After Graceland the group won several awards, including five Grammys. The sound is soft, full and based on voices alone. It shows how a West African or South African tradition reached world pop through a collaboration with a well-known pop artist.
artiest/paul-simon-en-ladysmith-black-ma.listen: Listen to Homeless. Notice the difference between the low, flowing choir voices and Paul Simon's solo voice, and how the harmonies follow one another.

artiest/paul-simonon.text:
Paul Simonon is an English bassist and visual artist, born in 1955 in Thornton Heath, in south London. He grew up in Brixton and Ladbroke Grove and actually wanted to be a painter; with a scholarship he studied at the Byam Shaw art school. In 1976 the guitarist Mick Jones asked him to join a new band. Simonon had never played an instrument. Jones's guitar lessons came to nothing, and so he became a bassist. Half a year later The Clash was complete, with Joe Strummer as singer. Simonon is said to have come up with the name of the band and helped determine how the group looked.

His bass playing came from reggae, which he had got to know through the Jamaican communities in London. Unlike many punk bassists, he played melodic lines that moved against the guitar. The best-known image of him is the photograph by Pennie Smith, in which he smashes his Fender bass guitar on stage during a concert in New York in 1979. That photograph became the sleeve of London Calling, with pink and green lettering as a reference to Elvis Presley's first album.

After the end of The Clash in 1986 Simonon started the band Havana 3am. Later he played bass in The Good, the Bad & the Queen, with Damon Albarn, and with Gorillaz, on Plastic Beach (2010) and during the tours. He is also an established painter with exhibitions of his own. In 2023 he made an album with the singer Galen Ayers.
artiest/paul-simonon.listen: In The Guns of Brixton, from London Calling, listen to the heavy reggae bass line: Simonon wrote and sang this song himself. Notice how the bass carries the melody and the guitar mostly plays short chords on the off-beat.
